brief.head: Wrong prescription
brief.text: Critics of Big Tech de­scribe ad­dic­tion ma­chines and echo cham­bers cor­rectly, Amit Varma said, but state con­trol of al­go­rithms would one day fall to the worst pos­si­ble per­son. {036-C04}

brief.head: Tyrants count heads
brief.text: Early states wanted peo­ple to tax and con­script, not ter­ri­tory, Ajay Shah said: “what every tyrant wants is more peo­ple”. So peo­ple voted with their feet. {036-C06}

brief.head: Fame is a curse
brief.text: Put any field under the mi­cro­scope, Ajay Shah said, and what fa­mous peo­ple loudly say turns out to be wrong. Correlations, care­fully read, are a path to in­sight. {036-C10}

brief.head: The 60 per cent fix
brief.text: A good state in­ter­ven­tion, Ajay Shah said, gets the job sub­stan­tively done, per­haps only 60 per cent, with the least co­er­cion, as­sum­ing re­al­is­tic state ca­pac­ity, or rather in­ca­pac­ity. {036-C11}

brief.head: Dear younger me
brief.text: Imagine send­ing a let­ter by time ma­chine to your younger self, Ajay Shah sug­gested. Ego in­sists you did ev­ery­thing right; hind­sight shows al­most ev­ery­thing could have been done bet­ter. {036-C16}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on how change really happens
lead.head: Slow and steady wins the republic

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 36

body: Amit Varma needed his cof­fee first. Then he picked up a ques­tion left over from the hosts’ episode on India’s re­form­ers: what kept those peo­ple fight­ing for decades, with no re­ward in sight? And how, more broadly, does change hap­pen?
Ajay Shah’s an­swer, over five chap­ters, was that change is slow, comes from more than one di­rec­tion, and can­not be rushed.
He began by pulling apart two things Indians tend to fuse. We are “ex­ces­sively statist”, he said, and say “India won the World Cup” as if the play­ers, the peo­ple and the state were one.
“Some bloke won some sports match. There is the peo­ple of India and there is the state. It’s good to sep­a­rate them.” {036-C01}
Almost all the truth, beauty and cre­ativ­ity lies in the peo­ple, Shah said, and so does most of the rot. If any­thing, he said, the state is less im­por­tant than the peo­ple.
## Both ends of the mar­ket

Varma once be­lieved pol­icy peo­ple would achieve noth­ing: work on the de­mand side, the peo­ple, and the state would fol­low. He has since changed his mind and thinks both ends mat­ter. Shah agreed that both are needed. Gay rights ad­vanced as states fol­lowed opin­ion polls; open­ing India to the world was an elite project, be­cause “anti-foreigner comes read­ily”.
## Progress on pro­ba­tion

Varma doubted the faith that his­tory bends to­wards progress, rest­ing as it does on a small sam­ple of cen­turies. Shah judged progress over the span of a sin­gle life, and found the 20th cen­tury a grim test.
“Social and po­lit­i­cal catas­tro­phe is al­ways pos­si­ble,” he said. {036-C05}
Democratic back­slid­ing, he added, is now hap­pen­ing in coun­try after coun­try.
## Left to right

The state, Shah said, changes through a pipe­line that runs left to right: data, re­search, rival so­lu­tions, pub­lic de­bate, ex­pert com­mit­tees, de­ci­sions and im­ple­men­ta­tion. Each stage needs dif­fer­ent knowl­edge, and a fail­ure at any stage kills the re­form.
“And there is no run­ning away from this pipe­line.” {036-C07}
Does it take 25 years? “Yes, but there is no other way,” Shah said. Even the 1991 trade re­forms, he told a scep­ti­cal Varma, rested on decades of ar­gu­ment among econ­o­mists.

Society moves dif­fer­ently: not through mega­phones, Shah said, but through “quiet, care­ful con­ver­sa­tions from one to an­other”. {036-C12} Each good con­ver­sa­tion shifts both sides by about 10 per cent.
For the cynic who would rather play his har­mo­nium while the world burns, Shah’s an­swer was self-interest. In Weimar Germany, a the­ory of the world told you when it was time to leave.
For ide­al­ists, his ad­vice was to pace them­selves, ask for no re­ward and treat the work as dharma. “We are all peb­bles in the avalanche,” he said. {036-C14}
Find fel­low trav­ellers who will do hon­est post-mortems and tell you when you are wrong, he added.

Shah rec­om­mended James C Scott’s *Weapons of the Weak*, on why many peo­ple sen­si­bly keep the state at a dis­tance. Varma, step­ping away from the state al­to­gether, chose the short sto­ries of Alice Munro.

second.label: Prehistory
second.head: Paradise lost to grain
second.deck: Ajay Shah, after James C Scott, on why farming made life worse

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the curse of agriculture

body: As chil­dren we are told that sav­age hunter-gatherers pro­gressed to agri­cul­ture and then to in­dus­try. Modern think­ing, Ajay Shah said, has turned that story around: given a choice of year to be born into, you would pick a hunter-gatherer one. {036-S04}
Hunter-gatherers were free, women were free and health was good. Male skele­tons reached six feet and fe­male ones five feet seven, heights not seen again until the 20th cen­tury. {#skeleton}

Agriculture brought dis­ease, shrink­ing heights, so­cial con­trol and women treated as prop­erty. Grain was cen­tral to early states, whose deal­ings with the peo­ple were tax­a­tion and con­scrip­tion. Drawing on James C Scott, Shah said many peo­ple sen­si­bly ran away. {036-C06}

quote.text: If you had to choose a year to be born into, you would al­ways choose a hunter gath­erer pe­riod.

third.head: Minds change by a tenth

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on three stages of persuasion

body: As a child, Ajay Shah be­lieved that show­ing some­one how Kepler’s laws fol­low from Newton’s would change the world at once and ban­ish su­per­sti­tion.
Then came many decades of gloom, he said, in which he thought peo­ple only talk past each other, smile po­litely, avoid con­flict and never change their minds.

Now he holds a mid­dle view. In a zone of truth and trust, peo­ple do hear each other. Nobody ad­mits de­feat, not even in their own heart, but in time the mind mulls things over and shifts by about 10 per cent. {#tenpercent}
“I will never be hon­est enough to say in front of you that you were right and I was wrong,” Shah said. “Okay, this is my human frailty.” {036-S06}

p2.title: The long game
p2.deck: How the state, society and each of us change, as argued by Amit Varma and Ajay Shah

from1.head: Slow and steady wins the republic

quote.text: change has to come from within so­ci­ety, it has to come from the bot­tom up.

box.title: The thinker behind the episode
box.text: James C Scott’s books on early states run through the episode. In *Weapons of the Weak* and *Against the Grain*, Ajay Shah said, states emerged to tax and con­script, and many peo­ple sen­si­bly kept them out of their lives. {036-R01}

sections.label: The first question
sections.head: India didn’t win the World Cup
sections.caption: the state and the people
body: When Indians say “India won the World Cup”, Ajay Shah said, they mix up three things: some play­ers, the peo­ple and the state. Indians are “ex­ces­sively statist”, he ar­gued, and for­get that the peo­ple mat­ter more. {036-C01}

Almost all the truth, beauty and cre­ativ­ity lies in the peo­ple, he said. So does much of the rot. The basic ques­tion should be how peo­ple can build cul­ture, as­so­ci­a­tions, firms and clubs them­selves, in­stead of run­ning to the mai-baap sarkar.

Amit Varma an­swered with Bertolt Brecht’s poem *The Solution*, about leaflets declar­ing that the peo­ple had squan­dered the government’s con­fi­dence: “Would it not in that case be sim­pler for the gov­ern­ment to dis­solve the peo­ple and elect an­other?” {036-J11}
## Topsoil

India, Varma said, began by as­sum­ing change would come from the top. Ambedkar de­scribed the con­sti­tu­tion as a mere top­soil over a deeply il­lib­eral so­ci­ety, and Madhav Khosla later spoke of its ped­a­gogic ef­fect. It can­not work, Varma ar­gued: many peo­ple stopped build­ing a bet­ter so­ci­ety, ex­pect­ing the con­sti­tu­tion to do it. {036-C03}

He once thought pol­icy peo­ple would achieve noth­ing, since the state re­sponds to the de­mand of the peo­ple. Now he be­lieves small changes at the sup­ply end can have a mas­sive im­pact. {036-C02} Shah of­fered two tem­plates: gay rights ad­vanced as states fol­lowed opin­ion polls, while glob­al­i­sa­tion in India was an elite, top-down project.
~ Neither host claimed pri­macy for ei­ther route. “I’m not try­ing to diss any­body,” Shah said.

quote.text: change has to come from within so­ci­ety, it has to come from the bot­tom up.

sections.label: The second question
sections.head: Don’t bank on the arc
sections.caption: whether progress is guaranteed
body: Martin Luther King said the arc of the moral uni­verse is long, but bends to­wards jus­tice. Amit Varma is no longer so sure. The op­ti­mism of Francis Fukuyama’s *The End of History?* in 1989, he said, has since re­versed. {036-J14} Belief in progress rests on a small sam­ple of cen­turies.

Ajay Shah granted the magic of the sci­en­tific rev­o­lu­tion, from Newton to Maxwell, rel­a­tiv­ity and Darwin. Elsewhere the story is darker. He called the stretch from agri­cul­ture in Babylon about 5,000 years ago to lib­eral democ­racy, prob­a­bly in 19th-century UK, “a dark regress”. {#babylon}
## One life as the yard­stick

Shah’s pre­ferred timescale is a sin­gle life. Take ran­dom 20-year-olds and 60-year-olds of the 20th cen­tury, he said, and for large frac­tions of them the rest of life went ter­ri­bly. The Weimar Republic’s flow­er­ing of free­dom in 1918 turned into Adolf Hitler in 1933. {#weimar}

His les­son is that so­cial and po­lit­i­cal catas­tro­phe is al­ways pos­si­ble. {036-C05} Dream of progress and work for it, he said, but do not slip into a “mil­len­nial fer­vour” that it is locked in.

~ Varma cited Thomas Jefferson on the price of lib­erty being eter­nal vig­i­lance. Shah re­called a framer of the US con­sti­tu­tion, whose name es­caped him, who said he had given “a re­pub­lic if you can keep it”. {036-J18}

quote.text: So you should never get lulled into the no­tion of progress. There are no guar­an­tees.

sections.label: The state
sections.head: Seven stages, no shortcuts
sections.caption: the policy pipeline
body: How does the state change? Through a pipe­line that runs from left to right, Ajay Shah said, and no­body can jump the steps. It be­gins with data. No amount of moral ur­gency can sub­sti­tute for it, and a moral panic is when the state rushes through its most op­pres­sive mea­sures. {036-C08}

Weak states fum­ble or sup­press their num­bers, so satel­lites help. Lights pho­tographed at 1.30am come from street lights, petrol sta­tions and com­mer­cial com­plexes, giv­ing a monthly map of pros­per­ity. “The bird in the sky sees the damn truth,” he said. {036-C09}

Research then re­fines the “crude oil” of data into knowl­edge. Next comes imag­in­ing so­lu­tions to gen­uine mar­ket fail­ures at the least cost in money or co­er­cion, which he called the same thing. “Ultimately the poi­son is co­er­cion.” {036-C11}
## Debate, then law

There must be rival ideas, be­cause “when there is only one game in town, you have surely a bad thing going”. A vig­or­ous pub­lic de­bate, which needs free speech, widens the Overton win­dow; ex­pert com­mit­tees le­git­imise rad­i­cal ideas; de­ci­sions are en­coded in laws; and or­gan­i­sa­tions are de­signed to carry them out. Skip a stage, Shah said, and the re­form dies there. {036-C07}
~ Each stage needs dif­fer­ent skills. “In a good coun­try, elected leg­is­la­tors write laws,” Shah said. “In a bad coun­try, the joint sec­re­tary writes the law.” {036-J03}

quote.text: No amount of moral fer­vour or ur­gency can sub­sti­tute for data.

sections.label: Society
sections.head: One WhatsApp uncle at a time
sections.caption: quiet conversations that shift minds
body: “You have con­tro­ver­sially said and mem­o­rably said, so­ci­ety changes one WhatsApp uncle at a time,” Amit Varma told Ajay Shah. “Kindly ex­plain.” {#whatsapp}

Shah began by re­stat­ing that the peo­ple mat­ter more than the state: all the wealth, art, truth and beauty are made by the peo­ple. Varma sug­gested the state could al­ways set up a com­mis­sion to com­pose a na­tion­al­is­tic raga. {036-J06}

Megaphone ad­vo­cacy on so­cial media, Shah said, “gets pre­cisely noth­ing done”. What changes minds is eye con­tact, a zone of truth and trust, and liv­ing as an ex­am­ple, be­cause peo­ple do as we do, not as we say. {036-C12}
## The ten per cent rule

No one con­cedes an ar­gu­ment aloud, he said, or even pri­vately. But given time, the mind mulls things over and moves about 10 per cent. Persuade ten peo­ple by 10 per cent on a cou­ple of im­por­tant things, and that is a great deal. {#tenpercent}
~ Varma spot­ted an open­ing. After the record­ing, he said, he would ask Shah for ten Diet Cokes, so that Shah, shift­ing by 10 per cent, would hand over one. “Isn’t that cun­ning of me?” {036-J04}

quote.text: Society changes in one great con­ver­sa­tion that gen­er­ates a ten per­cent up­da­tion for both sides at a time.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on quiet conversations that shift minds

sections.label: The self
sections.head: Keep going, ask nothing
sections.caption: endurance and the long haul
body: Amit Varma quoted the line from Kashinath Singh’s *Kashi Ka Assi*, in its fam­ily-friendly ver­sion: the world is going to hell, but I’m going to play my har­mo­nium. {036-J22}

Ajay Shah’s first an­swer was plain self-interest. “You may not be in­ter­ested in the world, but the world is in­ter­ested in you,” he said. {036-C13} In Weimar Germany, the job in 1918 was to hold off the na­tion­al­ists, and in 1933 to take your loved ones and run.
## Pace your­self

Idealists burn out, Shah said, by bang­ing their heads against “some mad bugger’s wall”. Apathy is no an­swer ei­ther. Treat the work as your dharma, ask for no re­ward, and ac­cept de­feat with­out bit­ter­ness. {036-C14}

Then find fel­low trav­ellers who will do hon­est post-mortems: cel­e­brate suc­cesses, ex­co­ri­ate fail­ures, cry to­gether, keep going. “You have to be the per­son that tells me that I’m full of shit,” he said. {036-C15}

A men­tor at the Ministry of Finance had a ca­reer track mapped out for Shah; he chose the world of knowl­edge in­stead. {036-S07} He has known the mis­ery of watch­ing his work go wrong again and again, and con­cluded that the world owes you noth­ing.
~ Varma had a quiz: who said he was not so smart, he just stayed with prob­lems longer? Shah could not guess. It was Albert Einstein.

quote.text: Our job is to build knowl­edge and keep push­ing and ac­cept some good things and bad things that will come out of it

portraits.caption: Albert Einstein
portraits.credit: Ferdinand Schmutzer / Adam Cuerden, public domain

quote.text: But then you just have to grow up and rec­on­cile that the world owes you noth­ing and the best ideas and dreams will go ter­ri­bly wrong, and that’s just how the world is.

p3.title: Stories from the long road
p3.deck: Four tales of patience, from the trade reforms to a turned-down apprenticeship

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s provocation, and Ajay Shah’s customs-duty reply
stories.head: An overnight reform, decades old
body: Amit Varma came armed with a provo­ca­tion. The 1991 re­forms, he said, hap­pened fairly quickly and with no pub­lic con­sul­ta­tion. Many good re­forms, he sug­gested, had skipped the long pipe­line Ajay Shah had just de­scribed.
Shah dis­agreed, and reached for one of his favourite ex­am­ples: the re­moval of cus­toms du­ties.

Since the 1960s, through the work of Bhagwati and Srinivasan and Manmohan Singh’s PhD the­sis, econ­o­mists had ar­gued ve­he­mently over trade bar­ri­ers. On the other side, Shah said, “there were al­ways the left­ies and the na­tion­al­ists”.
One by one the data came out and the re­search came out, and in con­fer­ence after con­fer­ence the re­form­ers won the de­bates.
By 1991, for a whole bunch of peo­ple, the ques­tion was closed: du­ties had to go from 350 per cent to 5 per cent. {#duty} All that was left was how to se­quence it.
“But there were ac­tu­ally like 20 years of in­vest­ment in the early stages of the pipe­line that led to that sim­ple clar­ity that trade bar­ri­ers have to go,” he said. {036-S01}

Not every re­form had such ground­work, Shah con­ceded, and many of those that lacked it worked out less well. The ground­work also grows the peo­ple who carry the knowl­edge, he said, “be­cause the joint sec­re­taries don’t know much”.

~ Varma promptly imag­ined the episode play­ing on a giant screen to a hall full of protest­ing joint sec­re­taries, and re­minded Shah, nurs­ing a bro­ken ankle, that he did not even have all his joints. {#jointsecs}
stories.why: Reforms that look overnight are usu­ally the vis­i­ble tip of decades of data, re­search and ar­gu­ment. The pipe­line can take 25 years, Shah said, and there is no other way. {#twentyfive}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the 1991 trade reforms

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s stress test for the idea of progress
stories.head: A century that broke its promises
body: Pick a 20-year-old or a 60-year-old at ran­dom from the 20th cen­tury, Ajay Shah sug­gested, and ask how the rest of their life went. For large frac­tions of them, ter­ri­bly.

There were two world wars, the Russian Revolution, Nazi rule and the threat of com­mu­nism and nu­clear war. The hope of 1989 gave way to Putin’s Russia, a near-miss in Poland and the de­cline of Hungary.
In China, Deng Xiaoping began a pro­gramme in 1978; in 2012 came Xi Jinping and ab­so­lutist one-man rule. {#deng} In 2022, large-scale land war re­turned.
~ India in 1947, with Gandhiji, Nehru, Tagore and Ramanujan, was “the star pupil” of the post-colonial world, Shah said. “And you know, look at where we’ve come.” {036-S05}
stories.why: Catastrophe is al­ways pos­si­ble, so progress should never be taken as locked in. Strive for a bet­ter world, Shah said, but stay “a lit­tle cold and care­ful and ner­vous about the world”. {#nervous}

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah, asked to name one mistake, goes back to 21
stories.head: The apprenticeship he turned down
body: Asked by Amit Varma what he would write to his 17-year-old self, Ajay Shah re­called a ques­tion a friend once put to him on an­other pod­cast, with zero no­tice: name one mis­take you have made in your life.
He went back to age 21. Fresh out of IIT, the econ­o­mist Kirit Parikh in­vited him to ap­pren­tice with him for a cou­ple of years, after which he could do a PhD or what­ever he wanted. {#kirit}
Shah, daz­zled by the glam­our of the United States and a PhD, turned him down and went abroad. In hind­sight, he said, it was “the dumb­est de­ci­sion imag­in­able”.
~ “Like I could have had a cou­ple of years ap­pren­tic­ing with him, like lit­er­ally get­ting one-on-one time with him four times a week,” he said. {036-S03}

quote.text: And that would have been the great­est ed­u­ca­tion in the world pos­si­ble.

stories.postscript: Shah first told the story on Episode 18 of the pod­cast *Jack of All Knowledge*.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on his biggest mistake

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the craft between an idea and a law
stories.head: From spectator to draftsman
body: It is one thing to think of in­fla­tion tar­get­ing, Ajay Shah said, and an­other to turn it into a law. He learned the dif­fer­ence him­self.
When the New Pension System was being made law, he un­der­stood the idea but was “clue­less” about its legal scaf­fold­ing. He could only watch the draft­ing as a spec­ta­tor. {036-S02}
By the time in­fla­tion tar­get­ing came along, he had the full legal knowl­edge. He could walk the whole path from mon­e­tary eco­nom­ics to draft­ing an agree­ment, and then a law. {#inflation}
~ That is rare, he said: most laws in India are poorly drafted, and most lawyers in India don’t know how to draft law. Drafting a good one is an “ex­otic skill in India”.
stories.why: Turning a good idea into re­al­ity needs a dif­fer­ent skill at each stage of the pol­icy pipe­line. Even an econ­o­mist who un­der­stood the idea had to learn the craft of legal draft­ing to see it through.

quiz.q: Why, according to Ajay Shah, do tyrants want people rather than territory?
quiz.a: More peo­ple to con­trol means more peo­ple to tax, con­script and op­press.

quiz.q: Who said he wasn’t so smart, he just stayed with problems longer?
quiz.a: Albert Einstein, whom Ajay Shah failed to guess de­spite Varma’s clues.

quiz.a: The econ­o­mist Kirit Parikh’s; Shah chose a PhD in the United States in­stead.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 36. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Albert Einstein (Ferdinand Schmutzer / Adam Cuerden, public domain); B. R. Ambedkar (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Martin Luther King Jr. (Associated Press, public domain); Francis Fukuyama (Gobierno de Chile, CC BY 2.0); Alice Munro (MacDowell, CC BY-SA 3.0).

shelf.title: Seeing Like a State
shelf.creator: James C Scott
shelf.why: Scott’s ac­count of how state schemes to im­prove the human con­di­tion fail when bu­reau­cra­cies can­not ‘see’ the so­ci­ety they rule, with a tool­kit (state leg­i­bil­ity, high mod­ernism, metis) you can apply al­most any­where.

shelf.title: Runaway
shelf.creator: Alice Munro
shelf.why: Munro’s sto­ries are set in one prov­ince of Canada yet cap­ture the human con­di­tion so well that read­ers ev­ery­where love her.

shelf.title: Hateship, Friendship, Courtship, Loveship, Marriage
shelf.creator: Alice Munro
shelf.why: Amit calls both col­lec­tions mas­ter­pieces and sug­gests them as a break from the state, eco­nom­ics and pol­i­tics, be­cause he be­lieves every good work of fic­tion speaks to the reader per­son­ally.

shelf.title: The Bear Came Over the Mountain
shelf.creator: Alice Munro
shelf.why: It is per­haps Amit’s favourite short story of all time, and he calls it ‘just magnificent’.

shelf.title: The Solution
shelf.creator: Bertolt Brecht
shelf.why: In a few lines it skew­ers a state that blames its peo­ple in­stead of serv­ing them.

shelf.title: Kashi Ka Assi
shelf.creator: Kashinath Singh
shelf.why: A line from Kashinath Singh’s book, about play­ing your har­mo­nium while the world goes to hell, gives Amit his stance on so­cial media: block the toxic ac­counts and build a feed of the finest minds.

shelf.title: The End of History?
shelf.creator: Francis Fukuyama
shelf.why: Fukuyama’s essay cap­tures the post-1989 be­lief that lib­eral democ­racy had won the ar­gu­ment for good.

shelf.title: Mera Joota Hai Japani
shelf.why: He in­tro­duces it, play­fully, as ‘a fa­mous song that is about the glory of globalization’.

shelf.title: The Reformers (Episode 28)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The human story of the peo­ple who worked be­hind the scenes, often for decades and with­out re­ward, to open India up in 1991.

shelf.title: The Ideas of Our Constitution (Episode 164 of The Seen and the Unseen, with Madhav Khosla)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It lays out the trans­for­ma­tive, top-down view of the Indian con­sti­tu­tion that Amit ar­gues against here.

shelf.title: India’s Massive Pensions Crisis (Episode 347 of The Seen and the Unseen, with Ajay Shah and Renuka Sane)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Ajay and Renuka Sane on the old ver­sus new pen­sion scheme: a bi­par­ti­san re­form built by a small in­tel­lec­tual com­mu­nity, and how in­sti­tu­tional mem­ory van­ished once that com­mu­nity dis­persed.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of KP Krishnan (Episode 355 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: An eight-hour oral his­tory from a re­former in­side the Indian state: how India han­dled the 2008 cri­sis, fought for in­fla­tion tar­get­ing and built the bank­ruptcy code.

shelf.title: Understanding the State (Episode 25)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The foun­da­tion of the show’s think­ing on gov­ern­ment: the state is a mo­nop­oly on vi­o­lence that acts through co­er­cion, so every in­ter­ven­tion, paid for by taxes, must be jus­ti­fied.

shelf.title: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on mar­ket fail­ure in its pre­cise tech­ni­cal sense (pub­lic goods, ex­ter­nal­i­ties and the rest) and on the nar­row con­di­tions under which the state may in­ter­vene, con­di­tions that are nec­es­sary but not suf­fi­cient.

shelf.title: We Love Vaccines! We Love Freedom! (Episode 27)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The third part of the state se­ries, ap­ply­ing its tool­kit to vac­cines: COVID vac­cine mak­ers were paid far less than the value they cre­ated, and let­ting prices rise would al­lo­cate vac­cines bet­ter and fund re­search for the next pan­demic.

shelf.title: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Episode 24)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why academia has drifted away from real-world prob­lems: jour­nal-based pro­mo­tion and de­part­men­tal in­cen­tives nar­row every dis­ci­pline, fil­ter out cre­ative mav­er­icks and leave aca­demics writ­ing for each other.

shelf.title: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Episode 33)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Explains that politi­cians and bu­reau­crats re­spond to in­cen­tives like ev­ery­one else, so the state is no benev­o­lent beast and gov­ern­ment fail­ure is far more com­mon than mar­ket fail­ure.

shelf.title: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335 of The Seen and the Unseen, with Ajay Shah)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A five-and-a-half-hour mas­ter­class from Ajay on the war and the deep his­to­ries of Russia and Ukraine, built on a life­time of read­ing and a counter to Russian pro­pa­ganda.

shelf.title: XKDR Forum paper and software on methodology for nighttime lights data (‘But clouds got in my way’)
shelf.creator: XKDR Forum
shelf.why: Ajay’s group’s paper doc­u­ment­ing a cloud-related bias in NASA/NOAA night­time-lights data, with a con­ser­va­tive cor­rec­tion; the data mea­sures pros­per­ity monthly at half-kilometre res­o­lu­tion with­out de­pend­ing on the gov­ern­ment.

shelf.title: Ajay Shah on state capacity, governance and institutions (Episode 18 of Jack of All Knowledge)
shelf.why: This is where Ajay first told the story of turn­ing down Kirit Parikh’s ap­pren­tice­ship offer.

laughs.text: Right after Ajay de­fends the value of cor­re­la­tions, Amit of­fers one: total hours watched of Everything is Everything have been ris­ing along with India’s GDP, so ‘the pros­per­ity of our na­tion re­lies upon us.’

Ajay: ‘In a good coun­try, elected leg­is­la­tors write laws. In a bad coun­try, the joint sec­re­tary writes the law.’ Amit then pic­tures this episode play­ing on a giant screen to a hall full of protest­ing joint sec­re­taries, adding: ‘And you of all peo­ple with a bro­ken ankle, you don’t even have all your joints.’

Amit ap­plies Ajay’s 10% the­ory of per­sua­sion: ‘right after this record­ing, I am going to ask you for ten Diet Cokes. So you change your views by ten per­cent and give me one. Isn’t that cun­ning of me?’
Ajay on Nazism: ‘Nazi stands for na­tion­al­ist socialism’, call­ing it two bad ideas fused into one.

When Ajay says the art and beauty all come from the peo­ple, Amit in­ter­jects that the state ‘can set up a com­mis­sion to com­pose a sonata. They can set up a com­mis­sion to come up with a new raga which is na­tion­al­is­tic.’

Amit claims he shifted the Overton win­dow of pod­cast du­ra­tion. His five- and six-hour episodes made two or three hours nor­mal: when he started, ‘one hour was con­sid­ered a deep dive’, and now ‘one hour is like a minia­ture.’
Riffing on ‘par­a­digms change one fu­neral at a time’, Amit re­calls Ajay’s line that ‘so­ci­ety changes one WhatsApp uncle at a time’.

Ajay opens with a line about the dia­lec­tic being in­ter­ested in you even if you aren’t in­ter­ested in it. Amit asks him to ex­plain it in sim­ple English, and Ajay obliges: ‘You may not be in­ter­ested in the world, but the world is in­ter­ested in you. There you go.’
Ajay on raw data with­out anal­y­sis: ‘there is data, data ev­ery­where, but not a thought to think.’

Bertolt Brecht’s ‘The Solution’, read by Amit: after the 17 June up­ris­ing, leaflets on the Stalinallee said the peo­ple had lost the government’s con­fi­dence. Brecht’s reply: ‘Would it not in that case be sim­pler for the gov­ern­ment to dis­solve the peo­ple and elect an­other?’

Martin Luther King’s ‘the arc of the moral uni­verse is long, but it bends to­wards justice’, and the say­ing that ‘par­a­digms change one fu­neral at a time’. Amit uses both to ques­tion the as­sump­tion that progress is in­evitable.

‘A re­pub­lic, if you can keep it’: Ajay re­calls this an­swer from a framer of the US con­sti­tu­tion but can’t re­mem­ber who said it. His point is that every gen­er­a­tion has to fight for its free­dom.

Amit quizzes Ajay on who said that he wasn’t so smart, he just stayed with prob­lems longer. Even with the clue ‘he’s one of your heroes’, Ajay can’t guess. The an­swer is Albert Einstein. Ajay adds that at 16 Einstein won­dered what the world would look like rid­ing a beam of light, and stayed with that ques­tion for years until it led to spe­cial rel­a­tiv­ity.
From Kashinath Singh’s Kashi Ka Assi, in its ‘fam­ily friendly version’: ‘Bhaad mein jaaye duniya, hum ba­jaayein harmonium’. The world is going to hell, but I’m going to play my har­mo­nium.
